messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Conflict: Confrontations, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event

Vignette:
Darren had been a plumber in North Carolina for more than two decades, the kind of man who could identify a leak by sound and spend a day under a sink without complaint. He was married now, living a quieter life than the one he had in his thirties, but the last few years had become organized around keeping himself out of situations that made his chest tighten and his thoughts scatter. The trouble had begun long before he sought help, back when he had been in a relationship with a man who could turn abruptly violent after an argument. Darren did not describe a single dramatic incident so much as a pattern of being cornered, shoved, struck, and then left trying to make sense of what had happened. What stayed with him most was the combination of fear and the sense that anger could arrive out of nowhere, even when it was spoken in an ordinary voice.

The most vivid memory he returned to was one evening when an argument escalated in the kitchen. Something on the stove had burned, and the smell of burnt food hung in the room while his partner kept coming toward him, voice rising. Darren remembered backing up, hearing the hard tone in the man’s words before he was hit. Since then, that smell had never been ordinary for him. If a pan scorched in his own kitchen, or if he passed a job site where insulation or wiring had overheated, he would feel his body go alert in a way he could not shrug off. He would glance around, tense in the shoulders, as if the room might suddenly turn dangerous. Burnt odors had become less a nuisance than a warning signal, one that pulled him back to the feeling of being trapped in that kitchen.

In the months and years that followed, Darren changed the way he moved through daily life. He had come to dread confrontations, even mild ones. A disagreement with a supplier, a customer irritated about a delayed repair, or a family discussion that involved raised voices could leave him feeling cornered and jumpy. What frightened him most was not only shouting but any expression of anger at all, even when it was controlled. If someone spoke firmly to a coworker, or if his wife sounded annoyed but was not actually upset with him, he could still feel himself bracing. He would read the tone for danger before he could understand the words. On jobs, this became especially difficult in small houses where he had to work in close quarters with irritated homeowners. He found himself eager to finish quickly and leave, sometimes making excuses to avoid lengthy conversations when a customer’s frustration showed in their face or voice.

Darren also began arranging his evenings around not having to think. When he got home from work, he kept busy with chores, television, or his phone until very late. He told himself he was just unwinding, but it was also a way of putting off the quiet moments when the memories came into view. If he sat still after dark, his mind would drift toward the relationship he had tried for so long to survive, and he would immediately try to push the thoughts away. He did not want to rehearse what had happened or imagine what he should have done differently. Thinking about the event felt like opening a door he had worked hard to shut. By staying up until long after his wife had gone to bed, he could avoid that stretch of the night when the house was silent enough for memories to crowd in. The habit cost him sleep and left him worn out in the morning, but he found the tradeoff easier than lying awake with his mind going back over the abuse.

Over time, he also stopped going near the place where much of the abuse had occurred. The site itself was not far from his current work routes, and on some drives he would catch sight of the street or the building and feel a sharp urge to turn away. He would choose a longer path, even when it meant extra time on the road, because being near it brought back too much at once: the sounds, the smell, the feeling of being trapped with someone whose anger he could not predict. He did not talk much about this to others, and at home he kept his responses contained, but his wife noticed that he slept poorly and that he became visibly tense around conflict in the neighborhood or at work. Darren knew he was putting strain on his life, yet he also felt that avoiding these situations had become the only way he could keep himself steady.

He finally sought help when the pattern began to feel harder to manage than to live with. A recent workday had started with the smell of something burnt in a customer’s kitchen, followed by an exchange with a homeowner whose irritation was not aimed at him but still sounded sharp enough to make him freeze for a moment. By evening he was exhausted, unsettled, and already planning how to stay up late so he would not have to sit with his thoughts. He came to treatment wanting relief from the constant need to steer around reminders, and he was most afraid that if he did not get help, he would keep shrinking his life further. At the same time, he hoped that he might finally be able to walk into a room with tension in it, smell something burnt, or hear an angry voice without feeling as though he had been thrown back into that kitchen again.
